title: Other religions
hook: the Vatican sends greetings for Vesak, Diwali and other feasts

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muslim neighbors, and the council's careful word for them. Your line was with esteem. Did you get to greet someone by name? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

A letter goes out from an office in Rome, addressed to Buddhist friends, for the feast of Vesak. Another goes out, addressed to Hindu friends, for Diwali, the festival of lights. They come from the Vatican's office for interreligious dialogue, and they read like letters between neighbors: good wishes for the feast, a few lines on something both communities care about, and an invitation to work together. Behind the letters sits one sentence from the Second Vatican Council. Today, other religions.
screen: `A LETTER FOR VESAK.` → `A LETTER FOR DIWALI.` → `ONE SENTENCE BEHIND THEM.`

segments.voice: The sentence is in Nostra Aetate, the same declaration as yesterday, a little earlier in the text. It says the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions. Rejects nothing true and holy. That's the root of the letters. Before it gets there, the council describes other paths in their own terms, with respect. Of Hinduism, it says people there contemplate the divine mystery and express it through myth and philosophy, and seek release through ascetic practice, deep meditation, and a loving, trusting flight toward God. Of Buddhism, it says it recognizes the insufficiency of this changing world, and teaches a way to reach perfect liberation or supreme illumination. The council isn't grading anyone. It's listening and describing. Then it adds a balancing line, in two halves. The Church looks with sincere respect on ways of acting and teaching that differ from its own, because they often reflect a ray of the truth that enlightens all people. And in the same breath it says the Church proclaims Christ, who in John's Gospel says, in the Douay-Rheims, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." Respect and proclamation sit in one paragraph. The council doesn't treat them as rivals. Finally, the council turns that into practice. It urges Catholics to enter into dialogue and collaboration with followers of other religions, with prudence and love, and to recognize and promote the spiritual and moral goods found among them. A letter for Diwali is one small way of doing exactly that. It doesn't say all paths are the same. It says: we see your feast, and we wish you well.
screen: `NOTHING TRUE AND HOLY IS REJECTED.` · `OTHER PATHS DESCRIBED IN THEIR OWN TERMS.` · `RESPECT AND PROCLAMATION, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `DIALOGUE, WITH PRUDENCE AND LOVE.` · then, large: `I AM THE WAY, AND THE TRUTH, AND THE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare a greeting for another faith's feast. Settle, and breathe. Let a name come: someone you know who keeps a feast you don't, Diwali, Vesak, Passover, Eid, Vaisakhi, Lunar New Year, whatever is real in your own circle. If you don't know when their feast falls, decide you'll find out. Then shape the greeting in your head, in plain words: the name of their feast, and that you wish them and their family well. Nothing more is needed. If you pray, you can hold their household before God. The bell holds the time.
Other religions. Nostra Aetate says the Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in them, and asks Catholics for dialogue with prudence and love. Today's word.

Your line: greetings of respect. Today, put one feast from another faith in your calendar, with a name next to it, so that when the day comes, a greeting goes out. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: A Vatican office for interreligious dialogue sends messages of greeting for feasts such as Vesak and Diwali, and some Catholic dioceses and parishes join local interfaith gatherings or send greetings to neighboring communities for their feasts.
